claim: Antiviral defense in ecdysozoan invertebrates requires Dicer with a helicase domain capable of ATP hydrolysis.
source: Antiviral defense in ecdysozoan invertebrates requires Dicer with a helicase domain capable of ATP hydrolysis.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known fact about ecdysozoan invertebrates and is supported by citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: Human Dicer is incapable of ATP hydrolysis despite well-conserved ATPase motifs.
source: But despite well-conserved ATPase motifs, human Dicer is incapable of ATP hydrolysis, consistent with a muted role in antiviral defense.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data and citations in the manuscript.

claim: Ancient Dicer possessed ATPase function that is stimulated by dsRNA.
source: Biochemical assays indicated ancient Dicer possessed ATPase function, that like extant invertebrate Dicers, is stimulated by dsRNA.
evidence: This claim is supported by biochemical assays performed on reconstructed ancestral proteins as shown in Figure 2.

claim: dsRNA stimulates ATPase activity by increasing ATP affinity, reflected in Michaelis constants.
source: Analyses revealed that dsRNA stimulates ATPase activity by increasing ATP affinity, reflected in Michaelis constants.
evidence: This is supported by Michaelis-Menten kinetic analyses presented in Figure 4 and Table 3.

claim: Deuterostome Dicer-1 ancestor retained some ATPase activity while exhibiting lower dsRNA affinity.
source: Deuterostome Dicer-1 ancestor, while exhibiting lower dsRNA affinity, retained some ATPase activity
evidence: This is supported by ATP hydrolysis assays and dsRNA binding experiments shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: ATPase activity was undetectable in the vertebrate Dicer-1 ancestor.
source: importantly, ATPase activity was undetectable in the vertebrate Dicer-1 ancestor, which had even lower dsRNA affinity.
evidence: This is demonstrated by ATP hydrolysis assays shown in Figure 2D and dsRNA binding data in Figure 3.

claim: Reverting residues in the ATP hydrolysis pocket was insufficient to rescue hydrolysis in vertebrate Dicer-1.
source: Reverting residues in the ATP hydrolysis pocket was insufficient to rescue hydrolysis, but additional substitutions distant from the pocket rescued vertebrate Dicer-1's ATPase function.
evidence: This is supported by experiments with AncD1VERT.1 and AncD1VERT.7 constructs described in the Results section and shown in Figure 4.

claim: Additional substitutions distant from the ATP hydrolysis pocket rescued vertebrate Dicer-1's ATPase function.
source: Reverting residues in the ATP hydrolysis pocket was insufficient to rescue hydrolysis, but additional substitutions distant from the pocket rescued vertebrate Dicer-1's ATPase function.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the AncD1VERT.7 construct showing rescued ATPase activity as shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Dicer lost ATPase function in the vertebrate ancestor due to loss of ATP affinity involving motifs distant from the active site.
source: Our work suggests Dicer lost ATPase function in the vertebrate ancestor due to loss of ATP affinity, involving motifs distant from the active site, important for coupling dsRNA binding to the active conformation.
evidence: This is inferred from the rescue experiments and Michaelis-Menten analyses showing high KM values for AncD1VERT.7.

claim: RIG-I-like receptors may have allowed or actively caused loss of ATPase function in Dicer by competing for viral dsRNA.
source: By competing with Dicer for viral dsRNA, RIG-I-like receptors important for interferon signaling may have allowed or actively caused loss of ATPase function.
evidence: This is a speculative evolutionary hypothesis based on the correlation between RLR evolution and loss of Dicer helicase function.

claim: Dicer is a multidomain endoribonuclease conserved in most eukaryotes.
source: Dicer is a multidomain endoribonuclease that is conserved in most eukaryotes (Jia et al., 2017; Gao et al., 2014; Fukudome and Fukuhara, 2017; Kidwell et al., 2014; Tabara et al., 2021; Bernstein et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Some organisms encode only a single Dicer.
source: Some organisms encode only a single Dicer (Bernstein et al., 2001; Kim et al., 2009; Ha and Kim, 2014; Watanabe et al., 2008; Li et al., 2016; Qiu et al., 2017; Ashe et al., 2013; Welker et al., 2010)
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies of various organisms.

claim: Some organisms encode multiple Dicers with different versions specialized for different functions.
source: while others encode multiple Dicers (Fukudome and Fukuhara, 2017; Kidwell et al., 2014; Lee et al., 2004; Cenik et al., 2011), with different versions specialized for pre-miRNA processing or endogenous/viral double-stranded (dsRNA) processing (Lee et al., 2004; Cenik et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2021; Wei et al., 2021; Deleris et al., 2006; Loffer et al., 2022; Poirier et al., 2018; Deddouche et al., 2008; Tsutsumi et al., 2011; Wu et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to studies showing functional specialization.

claim: Dicer contains an intramolecular dimer of two RNaseIII domains that cleave dsRNA.
source: Dicer contains an intramolecular dimer of two RNaseIII domains, the catalytic center that cleaves dsRNA.
evidence: This is a well-established structural feature of Dicer supported by citations.

claim: Dicer contains an N-terminal helicase domain, a platform/PAZ domain, a C-terminal dsRBM, and a DUF283 domain.
source: It also contains a platform/PAZ domain, an N-terminal helicase domain, a C-terminal dsRNA-binding motif (dsRBM), and a domain of unknown function (DUF283) with a degenerate dsRBM fold (Bernstein et al., 2001; Wei et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2018; Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by citations and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The size of the small RNA product is defined by the distance between the platform/PAZ domain and the RNaseIII domains.
source: The size of the small RNA product, either miRNA or siRNA, is defined by the distance between the platform/PAZ domain, which binds the ends of dsRNAs, and the RNaseIII domains (Wang et al., 2021; Park et al., 2011; Gu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to structural and functional studies.

claim: Dicer's helicase domain is capable of binding dsRNA termini.
source: Like the platform/PAZ domain, Dicer's helicase domain is capable of binding dsRNA termini
evidence: This is supported by citations to biochemical studies.

claim: The C-terminal dsRBM contributes to substrate binding and cleavage in some organisms.
source: and in some organisms, the C-terminal dsRBM contributes to substrate binding and cleavage (Wang et al., 2021; Su et al., 2022; Sinha et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to functional studies.

claim: Some extant metazoan Dicers have evolved substrate preferences where the platform/PAZ domain is specialized for binding 2-nucleotide 3' overhangs while the helicase prefers blunt termini.
source: To resolve this conflict, some extant metazoan Dicers have evolved substrate preferences where the platform/PAZ domain is specialized for binding the 2-nucleotide (nt) 3' overhang (3'ovr) of a pre-miRNA, while the helicase prefers dsRNA with blunt (BLT) termini (Welker et al., 2011; Sinha et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to biochemical studies.

claim: D. melanogaster Dicer-1 specializes in pre-miRNA processing but helicase function is not required.
source: In Drosophila melanogaster, Dicer-1 (dmDcr1) specializes in pre-miRNA processing, but helicase function is not required (Jiang et al., 2005)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a functional study.

claim: D. melanogaster Dicer-2 uses its helicase domain to recognize and bind viral and long endogenous dsRNAs.
source: while D. melanogaster Dicer-2 (dmDcr2), the second Dicer in fruit flies, uses its helicase domain to recognize and bind viral and long endogenous dsRNAs (Wei et al., 2021; Su et al., 2022; Sinha et al., 2018; Singh et al., 2021; Naganuma et al., 2021; Trettin et al., 2017; Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: dmDcr2 uses ATP hydrolysis energy for processive cleavage of dsRNA into siRNA products.
source: Once bound, these dsRNAs are threaded by the helicase domain to the RNaseIII sites, using the energy of ATP hydrolysis for processive cleavage into siRNA products.
evidence: This is supported by citations to mechanistic studies.

claim: dmDcr2's processive mechanism ensures that multiple siRNAs are produced from a single dsRNA.
source: This processive mechanism ensures that multiple siRNAs are produced from a single dsRNA (Su et al., 2022; Singh et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to mechanistic studies.

claim: C. elegans Dicer-1 requires a functional helicase domain to process long endogenous/viral dsRNAs.
source: Another invertebrate Dicer, Caenorhabditis elegans Dicer-1 (ceDCR-1), likewise requires a functional helicase domain to process long endogenous/viral dsRNAs
evidence: This is supported by citations to functional studies.

claim: C. elegans Dicer-1 processes pre-miRNA without a requirement for ATP.
source: but like dmDcr1, it also processes pre-miRNA without a requirement for ATP (Welker et al., 2010; Welker et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to functional studies.

claim: H. sapiens Dicer functions in an ATP-independent manner using its platform/PAZ domain to bind pre-miRNAs.
source: In contrast, Homo sapiens Dicer (hsDcr) has only been found to function in an ATP-independent manner, using its platform/PAZ domain to bind pre-miRNAs which are then distributively cleaved into mature miRNAs (Figure 1C; Liu et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The role of mammalian Dicer in antiviral defense is controversial.
source: Accordingly, the role of the single mammalian Dicer enzyme in antiviral defense is controversial
evidence: This is stated as a known controversy in the field.

claim: Sensing of cytosolic viral dsRNAs in mammals is primarily mediated by RIG-I-Like receptors.
source: as sensing of cytosolic viral dsRNAs is primarily mediated by RIG-I-Like receptors (RLRs), a family of enzymes that contain a related helicase domain (Loo and Gale, 2011; Goubau et al., 2013; Ahmad and Hur, 2015; Luo et al., 2011; van der Veen et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to immunology studies.

claim: Pathogenic dsRNA recognition by RLRs leads to production of interferon.
source: Pathogenic dsRNA recognition by RLRs leads to production of interferon, which in turn triggers production of multiple antiviral proteins to suppress viral replication (Loo and Gale, 2011; Rehwinkel and Gack, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to immunology studies.

claim: Helicase function in invertebrate Dicers correlates with a role in antiviral defense that seems to have been replaced by RLRs in mammals.
source: Thus, helicase function in invertebrate Dicers correlates with a role in antiviral defense that seems to have been replaced by RLRs in mammals.
evidence: This is an inference based on the functional differences between invertebrate and mammalian Dicers and the presence of RLRs.

claim: The ML tree displayed an early gene duplication event for HEL-DUF where ancestral animal Dicer was split into AncD1 and AncD2 clades.
source: The ML tree displayed an early gene duplication event for HEL-DUF, where an ancestral animal Dicer (AncD1D2) was split into two major Dicer clades, AncD1 and AncD2 (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in the phylogenetic tree in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: AncD1 contains the ubiquitous Dicer-1 found in most animal species.
source: AncD1 contains the ubiquitous Dicer-1 found in most animal species
evidence: This is inferred from the phylogenetic tree structure.

claim: AncD2 contains the arthropod-specific Dicer-2.
source: while AncD2 contains the arthropod-specific Dicer-2.
evidence: This is inferred from the phylogenetic tree structure.

claim: The observed gene duplication is consistent with previously reported phylogenetic analyses of full-length Dicer.
source: The observed gene duplication is consistent with previously reported phylogenetic analyses of full-length Dicer, suggesting that the HEL-DUF region contained enough phylogenetic signal to recapitulate broad patterns of Dicer evolution (Jia et al., 2017; Gao et al., 2014; Mukherjee et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous phylogenetic studies.

claim: The ML tree was not congruent with the species tree in multiple instances.
source: Importantly, we observed multiple instances where our ML tree was not congruent with the species tree.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the phylogenetic analysis.

claim: Incongruences in the phylogeny could stem from long branch attraction artifacts from the Dicer-2 clade.
source: We observed several incongruences in the phylogeny that could stem from long branch attraction artifacts from the Dicer-2 clade, which has undergone rapid evolution under the selection pressure of viral defense and may not have diverged as early as it appears in the phylogeny (Kolaczkowski et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed phylogenetic incongruences, supported by a citation.

claim: Constraining the ML tree to known bilaterian species relationships resulted in a few changes in the reconstructed sequences for AncD1D2 and AncD1DEUT.
source: To understand how changes in the phylogeny affect the predicted ancestral sequence, we constrained the ML tree to known bilaterian species relationships (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A), resulting in a few changes in the reconstructed sequences for AncD1D2 and AncD1DEUT.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A and Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: The variable amino acids between ML tree and species tree reconstructions are not predicted to significantly affect the observed biochemical properties.
source: However, the variable amino acids are not predicted to significantly affect the observed biochemical properties (96% identity between ML tree and species tree reconstruction; Figure 1—figure supplement 3A, B)
evidence: This is based on sequence comparison shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: APR performed using the species tree did not alter the AncD1VERT amino acid sequence.
source: and APR performed using the species tree did not alter the AncD1VERT amino acid sequence.
evidence: This is stated as a result of the comparative analysis.

claim: Constraining the arthropod Dicer-2 clade to a recent arthropod-specific duplication produces a more parsimonious tree with worse likelihood scores.
source: Finally, constraining the arthropod Dicer-2 clade in the species tree to a recent arthropod-specific duplication event produces a more parsimonious tree with worse likelihood scores, with a log-likelihood score of –435,841 compared to –435,706 for the ML tree (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B; Jia et al., 2017).
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis with specific likelihood scores provided.

claim: AncD1VERT had more than 95% of sites with posterior probabilities of 0.8 or above.
source: AncD1VERT had more than 95% of sites with posterior probabilities of 0.8 or above, while older constructs had an average of 75% of sites with posterior probabilities above 0.8 (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4A.

claim: Ancestral constructs were expressed recombinantly using baculovirus in Sf9 insect cells and purified to 99% homogeneity.
source: Ancestral constructs were expressed recombinantly using baculovirus in Sf9 insect cells and purified to 99% homogeneity (Figure 1—figure supplement 4B; Sinha and Bass, 2017).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4B and supported by a methods citation.

claim: Protein identity was confirmed with LC/MS/MS.
source: Protein identity was confirmed with LC/MS/MS.
evidence: This is stated as a method used to confirm protein identity.

claim: AncD1D2 showed ATP hydrolysis activity.
source: We observed ATP hydrolysis in the most recent common ancestor of hsDcr and dmDcr2, AncD1D2 (Figure 2A)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2A with ATP hydrolysis assays.

claim: Extant animal Dicers with no dependence on ATP lost the capacity for ATP hydrolysis subsequent to AncD1D2.
source: leading to the important conclusion that extant animal Dicers with no dependence on ATP, such as hsDcr, lost the capacity for ATP hydrolysis subsequent to this period in animal evolution.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that AncD1D2 has ATPase activity while hsDcr does not.

claim: Basal ATP hydrolysis activity was present at low levels in AncD1D2 (kobs: 0.06 min–1).
source: Basal ATP hydrolysis activity was present at low levels in AncD1D2 (kobs: 0.06 min–1) and was improved upon addition of dsRNA (Figure 2A, Table 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2A and quantified in Table 1.

claim: Addition of BLT dsRNA to AncD1D2 promoted hydrolysis of ATP in the fast phase (kburst: 14.3 µM/min) and doubled the rate constant of the slow phase (kobs: 0.11 min–1).
source: Addition of dsRNA with BLT termini to AncD1D2, a substrate designed to mimic termini of certain RNA viruses, promoted hydrolysis of ATP in the fast phase (kburst: 14.3 µM/min) as well as doubling the rate constant of the slow phase (kobs: 0.11 min–1; Table 1).
evidence: This is quantified in Table 1 based on data from Figure 2.

claim: Similar rates were observed when 3'ovr dsRNA was used with AncD1D2.
source: Similar rates were observed when a dsRNA with a 2-nucleotide (nt) 3' overhang (3'ovr; pre-miRNA mimic) was used (Table 1).
evidence: This is shown in Table 1.

claim: Lack of dsRNA terminus discrimination in AncD1D2 suggests substrate promiscuity absent in modern Dicers.
source: Lack of dsRNA terminus discrimination suggests a substrate promiscuity that is absent in modern Dicers, where BLT dsRNA is the optimal substrate for the helicase domain (Sinha et al., 2018; Welker et al., 2011; Sinha et al., 2015; Singh et al., 2021).
evidence: This is an inference based on the data and supported by citations to studies of modern Dicers.

claim: AncD2ARTH was more efficient at hydrolyzing ATP in the absence of dsRNA than AncD1D2 and all other ancestors tested.
source: The arthropod Dicer-2 ancestor, AncD2ARTH, was more efficient at hydrolyzing ATP in the absence of dsRNA than AncD1D2 and all other ancestors tested (Figure 2B and E), showing a two-phase reaction resembling a dsRNA-stimulated reaction (kburst: 6.47 µM/min, kobs: 0.05 min−1; Table 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2B and E and quantified in Table 1.

claim: AncD2ARTH's efficient hydrolysis in the absence of dsRNA suggests it refined its ATP binding pocket to produce high affinity for ATP even without nucleic acid.
source: This efficient hydrolysis in the absence of dsRNA suggests that AncD2ARTH refined its ATP binding pocket to produce high affinity for ATP even in the absence of nucleic acid.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed kinetic behavior.

claim: Addition of BLT dsRNA to AncD2ARTH increased the rate of the fast phase (kburst: 19.3 µM/min) with slightly better efficiency compared to 3'ovr dsRNA (kburst:14.6 µM/min).
source: Addition of BLT dsRNA increased the rate of the fast phase (kburst: 19.3 µM/min), with slightly better efficiency compared to 3'ovr dsRNA (kburst:14.6 µM/min; Table 1, Figure 2B and F)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2B and F and quantified in Table 1.

claim: Terminus discrimination in AncD2ARTH foreshadows the terminus discrimination seen in modern dmDcr2.
source: perhaps foreshadowing the terminus discrimination seen in modern dmDcr2 (Sinha et al., 2015; Singh et al., 2021).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed preference for BLT dsRNA and supported by citations.

claim: Terminus discrimination was also observed in Dicer-1 ancestors.
source: Interestingly, terminus discrimination was also observed in Dicer-1 ancestors
evidence: This is based on the ATP hydrolysis data for Dicer-1 ancestors.

claim: The foundation of terminus discrimination existed in AncD1D2 even if not observable at the conditions tested.
source: suggesting the foundation of this discrimination existed in AncD1D2, even if not observable at the conditions tested.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of terminus discrimination in descendant lineages.

claim: AncD1DEUT had a pattern of basal and dsRNA-stimulated ATP hydrolysis similar to AncD1D2 with a reduction in overall hydrolysis efficiency.
source: The deuterostome Dicer-1 node immediately preceding vertebrate Dicer-1, AncD1DEUT, had a pattern of basal and dsRNA-stimulated ATP hydrolysis similar to AncD1D2 (Table 1; Figure 2C, E and F) with a reduction in overall hydrolysis efficiency
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2C, E, and F and quantified in Table 1.

claim: AncD1DEUT showed discrimination when triggered by different dsRNA termini (BLT, kburst: 6.0 µM/min; 3'ovr, kburst: 1.4 µM/min).
source: but the appearance of discrimination when triggered by different dsRNA termini (BLT, kburst: 6.0 µM/min; 3'ovr, kburst: 1.4 µM/min; Table 1).
evidence: This is quantified in Table 1.

claim: The reduction in ATP hydrolysis efficiency prior to deuterostome divergence may have coincided with or been caused by the appearance of innate immune effector proteins.
source: This reduction in ATP hydrolysis efficiency prior to deuterostome divergence may have coincided with, or may have been caused by, the appearance of innate immune effector proteins in invertebrate evolution.
evidence: This is a speculative evolutionary hypothesis.

claim: In AncD1VERT, ATP hydrolysis was undetectable.
source: Most importantly, in the ancestor of vertebrate Dicer, AncD1VERT, ATP hydrolysis was undetectable (Figure 2D)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Modern hsDcr is incapable of ATP hydrolysis.
source: consistent with observations that modern hsDcr is incapable of ATP hydrolysis (Zhang et al., 2002)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Loss of Dicer ATPase activity progressed further between the deuterostome ancestor and the vertebrate ancestor.
source: and indicating that loss of Dicer ATPase activity progressed further between the deuterostome ancestor and the vertebrate ancestor, probably driven by a collection of evolutionary events.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed loss of activity in AncD1VERT.

claim: An ancestral protein-based innate immune system existed prior to deuterostomes.
source: While an ancestral protein-based innate immune system existed prior to deuterostomes
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: The appearance of the interferon molecule and its expanded role in innate and adaptive immunity may have contributed to further loss of Dicer helicase function.
source: the appearance of the interferon molecule and its expanded role in innate and adaptive immunity may have contributed to further loss of Dicer helicase function and set the stage for miRNA expansion (Dehal and Boore, 2005; Secombes and Zou, 2017; Qiao et al., 2021; Berezikov, 2011).
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis supported by citations.

claim: All ancestral proteins bound dsRNA and showed multiple shifts that typically decreased in mobility with increasing protein concentration.
source: All ancestral proteins bound dsRNA and showed multiple shifts that typically decreased in mobility with increasing protein concentration.
evidence: This is based on EMSA data shown in Figure 3.

claim: AncD1D2 displayed tight binding to BLT dsRNA without ATP (Kd, 3.4 nM).
source: AncD1D2, the most ancient construct tested, displayed tight binding to BLT dsRNA without ATP (Kd, 3.4 nM)
evidence: This is quantified in Table 2 based on EMSA data.

claim: Addition of 5 mM ATP to AncD1D2 caused a twofold reduction in affinity for BLT dsRNA (Kd, 6.4 nM).
source: while the addition of 5 mM ATP caused a twofold reduction in affinity (Kd, 6.4 nM; Table 2, Figure 3B and H).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3B and H and quantified in Table 2.

claim: AncD1D2 binding to 3'ovr dsRNA was similarly tight with an ~twofold reduction in binding affinity compared to BLT.
source: Binding to 3'ovr dsRNA was similarly tight, albeit with an ~twofold reduction in binding affinity compared to BLT in the absence or presence of ATP (Table 2, Figure 3C and H).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3C and H and quantified in Table 2.

claim: dsRNA binding is the earliest point of terminus discrimination for ATP hydrolysis with ancestral HEL-DUFs.
source: This suggests that dsRNA binding is the earliest point of terminus discrimination for ATP hydrolysis with ancestral HEL-DUFs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed differences in binding affinity for different termini.

claim: The observed lower affinity with ATP may occur because ATP hydrolysis promotes dissociation or translocation that results in HEL-DUF sliding off dsRNA.
source: Possibly, the observed lower affinity with ATP occurs because ATP hydrolysis promotes dissociation or translocation that results in HEL-DUF sliding off dsRNA.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed effect of ATP on dsRNA binding.

claim: The more ancient the HEL-DUF construct in the tree, the tighter its interaction with dsRNA, regardless of the presence or absence of ATP.
source: An obvious feature evident from the binding isotherms (Figure 3H) was that the more ancient the HEL-DUF construct in our tree, the tighter its interaction with dsRNA, regardless of the presence or absence of ATP.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3H and quantified in Table 2.

claim: AncD1DEUT had a lower binding affinity for dsRNA compared to AncD1D2 (~10–50-fold).
source: AncD1DEUT, the common ancestor of deuterostomes, which include humans, had a lower binding affinity for dsRNA compared to AncD1D2, regardless of termini or the presence of ATP (~10–50-fold, Table 2, Figure 3D and H).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3D and H and quantified in Table 2.

claim: In AncD1DEUT, the ability to distinguish BLT and 3'ovr dsRNA largely disappeared.
source: In addition, the ability to distinguish BLT and 3'ovr dsRNA largely disappeared, and ATP had little effect on dsRNA binding (Table 2, Figure 3E and H).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3E and H and quantified in Table 2.

claim: The lack of discrimination in binding for AncD1DEUT does not match the sensitivity to dsRNA termini observed in ATP hydrolysis.
source: This lack of discrimination in binding does not match the sensitivity to dsRNA termini observed in ATP hydrolysis (Figure 2C), suggesting an additional discriminatory step exists between initial dsRNA binding and ATP hydrolysis.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparing binding and hydrolysis data.

claim: For some constructs but not others, ATP's effect on dsRNA binding may be muted or altered at the low temperatures where EMSAs were performed.
source: Another possibility is that for some constructs but not for others, ATP's effect on dsRNA binding is muted or altered at the low temperatures (4°C) where EMSAs were performed.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed differences.

claim: AncD1VERT binding to dsRNA resembled binding to AncD1DEUT in that affinity did not depend on termini or ATP.
source: Binding of dsRNA to AncD1VERT resembled binding to AncD1DEUT in that affinity did not depend on termini or ATP (Table 2, Figure 3F, G and H).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3F, G, and H and quantified in Table 2.

claim: AncD1VERT binding to dsRNA was weaker across all conditions with ~4.5-fold reduction in affinity compared to AncD1DEUT and ~30–150-fold reduction compared to AncD1D2.
source: However, AncD1VERT binding to dsRNA was weaker across all conditions with ~4.5-fold reduction in affinity compared to AncD1DEUT and ~30–150-fold reduction compared to AncD1D2 (Table 2).
evidence: This is quantified in Table 2.

claim: The Kd values measured for AncD1VERT were similar to values reported for the modern hsDcr helicase domain.
source: Interestingly, the Kd values measured for AncD1VERT were similar to values reported for the modern hsDcr helicase domain, or hsDcr with the platform/PAZ domain mutated to abolish competing binding, hinting that this construct correlates well with extant biology (Tian et al., 2014; Ma et al., 2012).
evidence: This is based on comparison with published values supported by citations.

claim: Between AncD1D2 and AncD1DEUT, HEL-DUF's dsRNA affinity may have decreased as the platform/PAZ domain began to play a more significant role in binding 3'ovr termini of pre-miRNAs.
source: One possibility is that between AncD1D2 and the deuterostome ancestor, AncD1DEUT, HEL-DUF's dsRNA affinity decreased as the platform/PAZ domain began to play a more significant role in binding 3'ovr termini of pre-miRNAs, and RLRs co-opted binding of virus-like BLT dsRNAs.
evidence: This is a speculative evolutionary hypothesis.

claim: Without added dsRNA, basal ATP hydrolysis for AncD1D2 had a kcat of 1117 min–1 and a KM of 35.8 mM.
source: Without added dsRNA, basal ATP hydrolysis for AncD1D2 had a kcat of 1117 min–1 and a KM of 35.8 mM (Table 3, Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and quantified in Table 3.

claim: Adding excess BLT dsRNA to AncD1D2 caused kcat to drop ~eightfold to 147.8 min–1 while KM dropped ~140-fold to 0.26 mM.
source: Adding excess BLT dsRNA caused kcat to drop ~eightfold to 147.8 min–1 while KM dropped ~140-fold to 0.26 mM
evidence: This is quantified in Table 3 based on Michaelis-Menten analysis.

claim: Binding of BLT dsRNA to AncD1D2 led to ~19-fold net improvement in kcat/KM.
source: indicating that although binding of BLT dsRNA to the AncD1D2 caused a reduction in the ATP turnover efficiency, it concurrently triggered a tighter association with ATP, leading to ~19-fold net improvement in kcat/KM (Table 3).
evidence: This is calculated from values in Table 3.

claim: The improvement in efficiency for AncD1D2 with dsRNA was primarily evident at lower ATP concentrations that fall in the range of intracellular ATP concentrations.
source: This improvement in efficiency was primarily evident at lower ATP concentrations that fall in the range of intracellular ATP concentrations (Patel et al., 2017; Figure 4A, right panel).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4A right panel and supported by a citation.

claim: dsRNA binding causes a conformational change in the helicase domain that allows tighter association with ATP.
source: At this 'lower' ATP concentration, we speculate that dsRNA binding causes a conformational change in the helicase domain that allows tighter association with ATP, enabling a more efficient hydrolysis reaction, until ATP concentration falls below a threshold where the reaction slows.
evidence: This is a speculative mechanistic explanation based on the kinetic data.

claim: For AncD1DEUT, basal hydrolysis proceeded with a kcat of 144.1 min–1, ~eightfold lower than the rate recorded for AncD1D2.
source: For the AncD1DEUT construct, basal hydrolysis proceeded with a kcat of 144.1 min–1, ~eightfold lower than the rate recorded for the AncD1D2 reaction (Table 3, Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C and quantified in Table 3.

claim: Association of ATP with AncD1DEUT was ~14-fold tighter than AncD1D2 leading to similar kcat/KM values for both enzymes in the absence of dsRNA.
source: Association of ATP with the AncD1DEUT construct, as measured by KM, was ~14-fold tighter leading to similar kcat/KM values for both enzymes in the absence of dsRNA (Table 3).
evidence: This is calculated from values in Table 3.

claim: Adding BLT dsRNA to AncD1DEUT caused a reduction in kcat by a factor of ~4 while reducing KM by a factor of ~8 to give a twofold net increase in kcat/KM.
source: Adding BLT dsRNA caused a reduction in kcat by a factor of ~4, while reducing KM by a factor of ~8 to give a twofold net increase in kcat/KM (Table 3, Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D and quantified in Table 3.

claim: Saturation of the helicase domain with BLT dsRNA caused improved ATP association to the catalytic ATPase site.
source: Thus, we observed a trend where saturation of the helicase domain with BLT dsRNA caused improved ATP association to the catalytic ATPase site.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed changes in KM values.

claim: It was impossible to confidently discern whether AncD1VERT produced a signal over background using the TLC-based assay even at 5 µM protein concentration.
source: However, even at higher protein concentrations (5 µM), it was impossible to confidently discern whether AncD1VERT produced a signal over background using our thin-layer chromatography (TLC)-based assay (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated as an experimental observation.

claim: AncD1VERT.1 with 20 amino acid reversions close to ATP binding/hydrolysis residues remained devoid of ATPase activity.
source: In AncD1VERT.1, we reverted 20 amino acids which were either close to ATP binding/hydrolysis amino acid residues or to the ATPase active site in the tertiary structure, but this construct remained devoid of ATPase activity (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated as an experimental result.

claim: In AncD1VERT.7, containing an additional 21 amino acid substitutions distant from the catalytic site, ATPase activity was rescued.
source: However, in AncD1VERT.7, a construct containing an additional 21 amino acid substitutions distant from the catalytic site, ATPase activity was rescued, and we measured its Michaelis-Menten kinetics.
evidence: This is stated as an experimental result shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Basal ATP hydrolysis for AncD1VERT.7 had a kcat of 257.7 min–1 and a KM of 61.7 mM.
source: Basal ATP hydrolysis had a kcat of 257.7 min–1 and a KM of 61.7 mM (Table 3, Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1E and quantified in Table 3.

claim: AncD1VERT.7 enzyme turnover was more efficient than AncD1DEUT but less efficient than AncD1D2.
source: Enzyme turnover was more efficient than AncD1DEUT but less efficient than AncD1D2, suggesting a rescue of the enzyme's inherent catalytic activity.
evidence: This is based on comparison of kcat values in Table 3.

claim: The high KM value for AncD1VERT.7 indicated that it was not rescued for tight association with ATP.
source: However, the high KM value indicated that AncD1VERT.7 was not rescued for a tight association with ATP, and the kcat/KM value for this construct was ~10-fold lower than kcat/KM for both AncD1DEUT and AncD1D2 (Table 3).
evidence: This is based on the KM value in Table 3.

claim: Adding BLT dsRNA to AncD1VERT.7 caused kcat to drop ~10-fold to 24.9 min–1 while improving the KM by ~12-fold, yielding no net improvement in kcat/KM.
source: Adding BLT dsRNA caused kcat to drop ~10-fold to 24.9 min–1 while improving the KM by ~12-fold, therefore yielding no net improvement in kcat/KM. (Table 3, Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1F and quantified in Table 3.

claim: ATPase activity was partially rescued in vertebrate HEL-DUF as well as the conformational changes that occur upon dsRNA binding.
source: Our observations indicate that we have partially rescued ATPase activity in vertebrate HEL-DUF as well as the conformational changes that occur upon dsRNA binding.
evidence: This is an inference based on the kinetic data for AncD1VERT.7.

claim: Amino acids distant from the ATP binding pocket were essential for resurrecting ATP hydrolysis in the vertebrate ancestor of Dicer.
source: Instead, we found that amino acids distant from the ATP binding pocket were essential for resurrecting ATP hydrolysis in the vertebrate ancestor of Dicer.
evidence: This is based on the comparison of AncD1VERT.1 and AncD1VERT.7 results.

claim: In the absence of dsRNA, hsDcr and dmDcr2 helicase domains primarily exist in an 'open' conformation with DUF283 wedged behind the Hel1 subdomain.
source: In the absence of dsRNA, hsDcr and dmDcr2 helicase domains primarily exist in an 'open' conformation, with DUF283 wedged behind the Hel1 subdomain (Figure 5A and B; Liu et al., 2018; Su et al., 2022).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5A and B and supported by citations to structural studies.

claim: dsRNA binding to dmDcr2's helicase domain causes a conformational change that brings DUF283 to the cleft of the helicase domain to clamp the dsRNA substrate.
source: dsRNA binding to dmDcr2's helicase domain causes a conformational change that brings DUF283 to the cleft of the helicase domain to clamp the dsRNA substrate (Figure 5C)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5C and supported by citations.

claim: In the closed conformation of dmDcr2, the distance between the 'DECH' box in Hel1 and the arginine finger motif in Hel2 is reduced from 13.28 Å to 4.26 Å.
source: In the closed conformation, the distance between the 'DECH' box in Hel1 (Motif II) and the arginine finger motif (Motif VI) in Hel2 is reduced from 13.28 Å to 4.26 Å (Figure 5D; Su et al., 2022).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5D and supported by a citation.

claim: The shorter distance in the closed conformation is predicted to be bridged by water, the attacking nucleophile for cleavage of the gamma-phosphate of ATP.
source: In helicases formed by two RecA domains, the shorter distance is predicted to be bridged by water, the attacking nucleophile for cleavage of the gamma-phosphate of the ATP molecule (Story and Steitz, 1992; Tian et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to mechanistic studies of helicases.

claim: The change in conformation is consistent with the reduction in KM values for ATP when BLT dsRNA is included in the ATP hydrolysis reaction for AncD1D2 and AncD1DEUT.
source: This change in conformation is consistent with the reduction in the KM values for ATP when BLT dsRNA is included in the ATP hydrolysis reaction for AncD1D2 and AncD1DEUT (Figure 4, Table 3).
evidence: This is an inference connecting structural observations to kinetic data.

claim: A KM of 14 µM was reported for the dmDcr2 ATPase reaction in the presence of BLT dsRNA.
source: Along the same lines, a KM of 14 µM was reported for the dmDcr2 ATPase reaction in the presence of BLT dsRNA (Cenik et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Excluding dsRNA would reduce dmDcr2's affinity for ATP, explaining why it does not hydrolyze ATP in the absence of dsRNA.
source: We predict that excluding dsRNA would also reduce dmDcr2's affinity for ATP, explaining why it does not hydrolyze ATP in the absence of dsRNA (Sinha et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a prediction based on the observed pattern in ancestral proteins and supported by a citation.

claim: AncD1VERT structures predicted by AlphaFold2 and RosettaFold have an open conformation while AncD1D2 resembles the closed conformation.
source: AncD1VERT structures predicted by AlphaFold2 and RosettaFold have an open conformation, while AncD1D2 resembles the closed conformation (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5E based on computational structure predictions.

claim: All the other ATPase-competent ancestral HEL-DUFs have a closed conformation.
source: All the other ATPase-competent ancestral HEL-DUFs also have a closed conformation (not shown).
evidence: This is stated based on structure predictions.

claim: The conformational differences between ancestral HEL-DUFs match the experimentally determined biochemical properties.
source: While these predictions are snapshots of a singular conformation from an ensemble of possible conformations, it is intriguing that the conformational differences between ancestral HEL-DUFs match our experimentally determined biochemical properties.
evidence: This is an inference connecting structural predictions to experimental data.

claim: In AncD1VERT, DUF283 is behind the helicase domain while AncD1D2's DUF283 caps the helicase cleft as in the closed conformation of dmDcr2.
source: In AncD1VERT, DUF283 (teal) is behind the helicase domain while AncD1D2's DUF283 (violet) caps the helicase cleft as in the closed conformation of dmDcr2 (Figure 5E, left panel).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5E left panel.

claim: AncD1VERT's Hel1 leans away from the Hel2-Hel2i rigid body by 31.8° compared to AncD1D2's Hel1 subdomain.
source: However, AncD1VERT's Hel1 (green) leans away from the Hel2-Hel2i rigid body by 31.8° compared to AncD1D2's Hel1 subdomain (red; Figure 5E, right panel).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5E right panel based on structure predictions.

claim: The difference in conformation affects the ATP binding pocket showing a wider distance between helicase motif II and motif VI in AncD1VERT compared to AncD1D2.
source: This difference in conformation affects the ATP binding pocket which exists at the interface between Hel1 and Hel2, showing a wider distance between helicase motif II and motif VI in AncD1VERT compared to AncD1D2 (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5F based on structure predictions.

claim: The wider distance between motifs in AncD1VERT may explain why it is incapable of basal hydrolysis even when catalytic motifs are repaired in AncD1VERT.1.
source: This may explain why AncD1VERT is incapable of basal hydrolysis even when catalytic motifs are repaired in AncD1VERT.1.
evidence: This is an inference connecting structural observations to experimental results.

claim: Non-catalytic motifs that affect conformation and helicase subdomain movement mediate the loss of ATPase function in vertebrate Dicer's helicase domain.
source: Our studies indicate that non-catalytic motifs that affect conformation and helicase subdomain movement mediate the loss of ATPase function in vertebrate Dicer's helicase domain.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the rescue experiments and structural analysis.

claim: The full-length ancestral animal Dicer was capable of binding dsRNAs at two sites: the platform/PAZ domain for pre-miRNA and HEL-DUF for long endogenous or viral dsRNA.
source: In our favorite model for Dicer evolution (Figure 6), the full-length ancestral animal Dicer was capable of binding dsRNAs at two sites: the platform/PAZ domain for pre-miRNA and HEL-DUF for long endogenous or viral dsRNA (Jia et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a model shown in Figure 6 and supported by a citation.

claim: Ancestral Dicer was probably more promiscuous and possessed the ability to translocate dsRNA from helicase to platform/PAZ.
source: This Dicer was probably more promiscuous and possessed the ability to translocate dsRNA from helicase to platform/PAZ.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the observed properties of ancestral proteins.

claim: After duplication, arthropod Dicer-2 evolved to a one-site mechanism where the HEL-DUF became the primary site of dsRNA recognition.
source: After duplication, arthropod Dicer-2 evolved to a one-site mechanism where the HEL-DUF became the primary site of dsRNA recognition.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed properties and supported by citations.

claim: Compared to the Dicer-1 clade, the platform/PAZ domain in arthropod Dicer-2 lost affinity for dsRNA.
source: This idea is supported by previous work showing that compared to the Dicer-1 clade, the platform/PAZ domain in arthropod Dicer-2 lost affinity for dsRNA (Jia et al., 2017)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Analyses of Drosophila species revealed evidence of positive selection in Dicer-2 HEL-DUF domains.
source: and analyses of Drosophila species that revealed evidence of positive selection in Dicer-2 HEL-DUF domains (Kolaczkowski et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: dsRNA and ATP binding to dmDcr2's helicase domain drive conformational changes in the entire enzyme and lead to translocation of dsRNA to the RNaseIII domain for cleavage.
source: Thus, dsRNA and ATP binding to dmDcr2's helicase domain drive conformational changes in the entire enzyme and leads to translocation of dsRNA to the RNaseIII domain for cleavage (Su et al., 2022; Singh et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to mechanistic studies.

claim: Drosha appears early in animal evolution and may have contributed to Dicer-1 specialization by performing processing of pri-miRNAs.
source: Drosha appears early in animal evolution and may have contributed to Dicer-1 specialization by performing processing of pri-miRNAs, a step performed by Dicer's helicase domain in plants (Moran et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis supported by a citation.

claim: Dicer-1 underwent a series of evolutionary changes between AncD1D2 and AncD1DEUT, culminating in vertebrate Dicer's helicase domain losing affinity for both dsRNA and ATP.
source: Dicer-1 underwent a series of evolutionary changes between AncD1D2 and AncD1DEUT, culminating in vertebrate Dicer's helicase domain losing affinity for both dsRNA and ATP.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing progressive loss of function.

claim: The decline in helicase function coincides with the appearance of the antiviral RLRs and interferon-like cytokines.
source: This decline in helicase function coincides with the appearance of the antiviral RLRs and interferon-like cytokines and may have facilitated subsequent miRNA expansion in vertebrates and mollusks.
evidence: This is a speculative evolutionary hypothesis.

claim: Vertebrate Dicer works with a one-site mechanism where the platform/PAZ domain is the predominant binding site for all its dsRNA substrates.
source: Thus, vertebrate Dicer works with a one-site mechanism where the platform/PAZ domain is the predominant binding site for all its dsRNAs substrates.
evidence: This is an inference based on the loss of helicase function and known properties of vertebrate Dicer.
